analysis.one_liner: Makes tenant protections for renters in foreclosed homes permanent and lets them sue to enforce them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2009 law gives renters in foreclosed homes the right to stay through the end of their lease, or at least 90 days, before a new owner can take over. That law was set to expire, leaving tenants facing quick evictions when their landlord lost the home. This bill would have removed that expiration date and added a new right: tenants wrongfully evicted could sue in court and recover attorney fees if they won.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in homes that go into foreclosure. The 2009 law they rely on was scheduled to lapse, so without a permanent extension, tenants would again face losing their homes with little notice when a lender or investor foreclosed and took possession. The bill also gave them a practical way to enforce those rights in court, with attorney fees paid by the violator if the tenant wins.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset provision of the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009, removing its December 31, 2012 expiration and making the tenant protections permanent [S2].

Adds a private right of action: any person harmed by a violation of the Act can sue for damages and equitable relief, and a prevailing tenant is awarded litigation costs, attorney fees, and expert witness fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders, servicers, and investors who take ownership of foreclosed homes, who would have to honor existing leases or give tenants at least 90 days before taking possession, and who could be sued with fee-shifting if they violate the rules. Purchasers at foreclosure sales also bear the cost of acquiring property subject to a tenant's remaining lease.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders and buyers of foreclosed homes

drawbacks.text: The fee-shifting provision creates litigation exposure: a buyer of a foreclosed property, including a small landlord with a legitimate title or notice dispute, could face a lawsuit where losing means paying the tenant's attorney and expert fees [S3].

A good-faith objection is that a permanent federal rule overlays state landlord-tenant law and constrains what buyers at foreclosure sales can do with property they lawfully purchased, including their ability to move in themselves or use the home; the bill offered no carve-outs for owner-occupant buyers in its enforcement section [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is modest and well-targeted: it does not stop the foreclosure or erase the debt, it just gives the tenant time to relocate or stay out their lease, and it preserves an existing law rather than creating a new program. The main cost falls on whoever takes the property after foreclosure, which is real but limited to the transition period. The enforcement mechanism with fee-shifting carries some risk of litigation against small buyers, but fee-shifting is a standard device in federal civil-rights and consumer statutes to make rights enforceable for people who could not otherwise afford a lawyer. On balance, the benefits to displaced renters outweigh the costs to property acquirers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2011, referred to the Financial Services Committee and then to a housing subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on December 8, 2011, with Rep. Pete Stark joining as the named original cosponsor [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced [S5].

On January 12, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity, which is where the record ends; the bill received no further action for the rest of the 112th Congress [S5].
The bill had 26 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support ever appeared in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the protections were left to expire on schedule, lenders, servicers, and investors acquiring foreclosed homes came out ahead: they kept the ability to take possession and remove tenants quickly, while renters in foreclosed homes lost the shield the bill would have made permanent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders and investors in foreclosed homes

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2009 tenant protections permanent and added a private right of action to enforce them.

for.name: 26 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat, and no Republican signed on.

against.name: Spencer Bachus
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee never held a markup or hearing on it, and it was instead routed to a subcommittee where no action followed.

against.name: Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 12, 2012 and took no further action on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 supporters in the record were Democrats (the sponsor and 26 cosponsors), with zero Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committee process produced no action [S4].

industries.industry: Lenders, mortgage servicers, and banks holding foreclosed properties
industries.note: The bill would have permanently required them, as new owners of foreclosed homes, to honor leases or give tenants 90 days, with lawsuit and fee exposure for violations. Their interest in taking possession quickly ran directly against tenants' ability to stay in their homes.

industries.industry: Real estate investors buying homes at foreclosure sales
industries.note: Purchasers at foreclosure sales would inherit tenants with remaining leases and could face damages suits with attorney fees attached. This is the group whose acquisition costs the bill directly raised.

industries.industry: Tenant-side attorneys and legal aid providers
industries.note: The private right of action with fee-shifting would have created enforceable cases for renters and paid counsel who took them. Their interest ran alongside tenants' interests.
